en: I bow with devotion to Him whose feet are honored by the lords of Daityas, men, and serpents, and whose toes— with their tips kissed by the luster of Indra’s crown— are touched by the heads of those [lords] who are languid from the great weight of their devotion.

May that Blessed One, the benefactor of the world and the best among the upholders of Dharma, protect us— he who did not bow to anyone, having himself awakened to the Dharma; he by whom the tree of all defects has been utterly uprooted through sleeplessness.

May that Buddha—whose birth, which is the source of affliction, calamity, wretchedness, fear, and suffering, has been exhausted; whose eye of wisdom has uprooted the entire mass of faults; and who is the sole kinsman of the world—be my refuge. 11.1.2
Victorious is the benefactor of the world, the teacher of the three realms of existence, the remover of the fear of manifold sufferings;
the friend of the world, who performs deeds most difficult to accomplish for the welfare of the world.
May that Blessed One be your refuge—he, the Master who unties the knots of the doctrines of evil sects.

Victorious is Dharma, the destroyer of the root of existence and the guide through the wilderness, who is uniquely skilled at tearing asunder the dense veil of doubt— the eggshell of delusion. Possessed by him,
a person conquers even Death, who is otherwise difficult to overcome.
I pay homage to that Buddha, the kinsman of the world, who out of compassion wandered through the ocean of existence for three incalculable eons and yet never succumbed to weariness; he,
having attained the cessation of all afflictions, no longer undergoes the burning of faults.
I bow to that Dharma, the cooling state, the teacher of the Lord of Munis.
(7) Let there be repeated homage to the Sangha, the pure treasury of a multitude of virtues, in whom the simultaneous arising of all meditative attainments is possible. (8)
It is the ruin of beauty, the burning of strength, the slaughter of all the senses;
it is the source of sorrow and the cessation of pleasure, a treasury for those things that dwell in the mind.
It is the destruction of knowledge, the humiliation of memory, and the abode of physical exhaustion.
That which drank in the world like the radiance of the sun was not extinguished in the world.

That [body] which, while in its youth, was capable of enduring vows, restraints, asceticism, and the study of sacred texts, and was well-suited for the hardships of warding off cold, heat, hunger, and thirst— || 11.1.9 ||

Worn out by the passage of time, my body— with its strength of sight, hearing, and memory impaired— is drained of its essence and, like a great carriage with broken parts, no longer carries me forward.
Even those whose memory and strength possess incomparable qualities [are likewise affected].
Even those who have never before been defeated in battles against the lords of elephants,
when overcome by old age and rendered helpless, lose their memory, their strength, and all their prowess. (11.1.11)
Having squeezed out its essence like the crushing of sugarcane, old age makes the embodied being withered,
and casts him into the mouth of death, as dry wood is cast into the domain of fire.
Death seizes and carries away one who is exhausted, drained of essence, and powerless— just as a king, having destroyed a region ravaged by calamities, takes it from which the heroes have perished;
breaking through the embankments of rivers and uprooting trees like tender sprouts.
Having slain rival elephants with their trunks, feet,
and tusks while they were arrogant with rut,
[elephants] reach old age— ignoble and causing hatred among young men.
This very same elephant endures the insults of young elephants;
he who was once deluded, burning with passion, afflicted by many various diseases, and dull-witted with exhausted senses— Subhāṣitāvalī 631.

With drooping limbs, groaning, struck down, with unblinking eyes, afflicted by suffering, helpless, lying upon his bed, incapable of any action, and like a figure painted on a canvas—whomever a person sees in such a state, even he experiences that suffering; he does not share his agony with elders or children. (11.1.14)
The ancestors remove the disease of their sons if they themselves do not suffer from illness, or if they share equally in that affliction;
for a man’s own self alone truly knows his own suffering.
To whom does the self belong? On this earth, whose are the sons? Sons desire to take away death or disease from their fathers, and fathers likewise [desire to take them] from their sons.
Nor does this world of living beings go to its mutual destruction by means of its own actions; [it is] Time that [acts] within food. 11.1.16.
In the *Anne*: Time.
Life is like an autumn cloud; pleasures are equal to the essence of a tree in full bloom;
and the enjoyments of the senses are as fleeting as the delights of a dream.
For all this is delightful merely by the power of one's imagination.
This other [teaching] is a rain of water for those suffering from thirst— cooling, quelling intoxication, and removing the heat of the intensified afflictions.

"Drink [this] with the vessels of your ears, being turned toward the sūtras of the Sugata; having purified your minds here, [drink] from the clouds of the One who possesses the Ten Powers. Thus [it is said].
§1 Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks:

“Monks, there are these three things that are undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable to the world. What are the three? Namely, sickness, old age, and death. For if these three things—sickness, old age, and death—were not undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable in the world, then Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones would not appear in the world, nor would the teaching and discipline proclaimed by the Tathāgata be established in the world.”

"Therefore, monks, because these three things are undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable to the world—namely, sickness, old age, and death—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones arise in the world; and for that reason, the teaching of the Dharma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is made known in the world."
The Blessed One said this; having said this, the Sugata, the Teacher, then spoke further as follows:
"Indeed, the brilliantly adorned chariots of kings wear out, and even the body undergoes decay."
But the dharma of the virtuous does not undergo decay,
for the virtuous proclaim it among the virtuous.
(Udānavarga 1.28)
Fie upon you, O vulgar old age; for you are indeed the maker of deformity.
For as long as you do not crush it, the physical form remains enchanting.
(Udānavarga 1.29)
Even he who lives for a hundred years is destined for death;
old age pursues him and strikes him down, whether it be through disease or the Ender himself. (11.2.3) [Note:
*anvety enaṃ*]

The Blessed One said this; and what was spoken by the Blessed One was spoken by the Arhat: "Monks, these four things are desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the world, yet all of them end in what is undesired. What are the four? Health, monks, is desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the world, yet all health ends in illness. Illness is undesired, unlovely, unpleasant, and displeasing to the world."

Youth is desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the world; yet all youth ends in old age. Old age is undesired, unlovely, unpleasant, and displeasing to the world. Life is desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the world; yet all life ends in death. Death is undesired, unlovely, unpleasant, and displeasing to the world. Prosperity is desired, lovely, dear, and pleasing to the world.
And every prosperity ends in misfortune; misfortune is undesirable, unlovely, unpleasant, and disagreeable to the world.
The Blessed One said this; having spoken thus, the Sugata, the Teacher, further said this:
Health is impermanent, youth is impermanent,
prosperity is impermanent, and even life itself is impermanent; for a living being who is struck down by impermanence, [what stability can there be]?
"How does delight arise in the strands of sensual pleasure?
The Blessed One said this, and those monks, their minds uplifted, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.
Acting like an immortal out of a wretched attachment to sense-objects,
why, intoxicated by the pride of life, do you not see the danger before you? While your vital organs are being cut away and your joints are being severed—
You ought to inflict upon his heart that very suffering which belongs to one who is dying,
while his vision is being drawn away and his consciousness is being carried off.
For one pierced by the dart of death, there is indeed no protector.
"Bound by the noose of Time, you will abandon your kinsmen as a helpless man;
oppressed by hiccup and parched by labored breath. (Śivagītā 8.58)
For one being dragged [along], there is indeed no refuge whatsoever. Mounted upon the wheel of saṃsāra, he is presided over by the messengers of Yama.
Afflicted by suffering, he does not find refuge, wondering, "Where shall I go?
There is no eye equal to wisdom; there is no darkness equal to delusion.
There is no enemy equal to disease; there is no fear equal to death. Therefore, since this most dreadful death must inevitably be encountered, [one should strive for liberation].
O son, since sensual desires must inevitably be relinquished, withdraw your mind from them and take delight in the true Dharma.
(Vararuci Gāthāśataka 96)
Neither a friend, nor a circle of kinsmen,
nor wealth acquired with effort, nor pleasures, nor enjoyments come to him at that moment, having abandoned hundreds of dear things.

The vital breaths depart, taking with them the path of food that is the fruit of one's own actions. In this world, both the enemy and the master alike close their eyes once wealth has been acquired through great effort.
But one thing alone, like a shadow following a traveler, cannot be taken away by others: it is karma itself.
The warriors return to their own homes, and likewise the ministers depart.
That multitude of women which does not follow even a single step behind him,
and the citizens along with the city itself, together with their stores of elephants, horses, chariots, and wealth,
simply remain where they are; for it is one's own past actions that truly follow a man.
In this world that is like an illusion, to whom could the claim "this is my mother, my father, my elder, or my kinsman" belong? This is from the *Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā* (later identified by Matsuda).
When this person goes forth alone, preceded by their own karma,
the world of the living is indeed like a tree providing shade for rest.
Every evening they gather at the banyan tree,
and every morning they depart by their respective ways.
Just as birds leave one another and that tree,
so too do kinsmen leave their kinsmen.
Life is as flickering as a wave upon the water;
worldly prosperities yield the fruit of many calamities.
Fleeting are meetings with beloved people; perform the accumulation of merit with devotion.
Like a beast yoked for the sake of carrying a load, [you are bound by worldly ties].
Like a fish in water caught in a net,
or like a herd of deer surrounded by a snare, the world remains powerless, standing on the verge of death. 11.3.15
Those lamps consisting of sūtras which were established by the Buddha after he had attained supreme enlightenment,
constantly piercing the darkness of ignorance—

May the flame of the Dharma blaze unshakably throughout the worlds— meaning, may the torch of the Dharma burn for a long time, even though the Teacher of the World has long since attained final nirvāṇa.
The dispeller of the cataract of ignorance illuminates both the even and the uneven.
May those gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas,
gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and humans who have come here to hear the Dharma protect this world and the teaching of the Jina.
And let them constantly practice the Dharma taught by the Lord of Sages.
